clue.text: Crikey, Bunter left hardly any!

definitions.meaning: an exclamation of surprise, the schoolboy Billy Bunter's favourite cry
greedy Billy Bunter leaves only tiny fragments of the food he has eaten

explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the greedy fat schoolboy of Frank Richards' British comic stories, famous for his cry of surprise and his appetite.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a mild British exclamation of surprise and the tiny fragments left after eating cake or bread.

clue.text: A smack on the wrist

definitions.meaning: a light slap or blow with the hand
the end of a sleeve that sits at the wrist

explanation.definitionFit: A light blow is a clip round the ear, and the shirt band at the wrist has the same name.

clue.text: Tear off a strip to do hair so it doesn't hang down

parts.note: hair that does not hang down is worn up
to braid is to plait hair

explanation.surface: A hairdresser is told how to style hair so that it is pinned up rather than loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear off a strip' is an idiom for scolding someone, not a hairdressing instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To tear a strip off someone is a British idiom for telling them off severely, a synonym of scold.

clue.text: What's missing in a fight is obscure

indicators.note: the word for what is missing is placed inside the word for a fight

parts.note: a bout is a boxing match
what is missing is a lack

explanation.surface: Something absent from a boxing match is said to be unclear.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at being knocked senseless in a boxing match, which is the answer's other meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To obscure a light or view is to darken it completely, as wartime windows were covered at night.

clue.text: Assigns to berth in stormy seas

indicators.note: the bed word is set inside the jumbled letters of the sea word
stormy seas are tossed about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: a berth is a bed, and a crib is a small bed

explanation.surface: Someone allocates passengers to their bunks while the sea rages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to berth' reads like mooring a ship in a storm; the berth is a bed, and the anagram of the sea word splits around it.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascribe something to someone is to attribute or assign it to them, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Ongoing panic

parts.note: read 'Ongoing' as 'on going', the fear felt by a performer about to go on in front of an audience

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ongoing' usually means continuing; split it as 'on-going' and it is a performer walking out before the audience.
explanation.definitionFit: The nervous dread of an actor before appearing in front of an audience is exactly a panic about going on.

clue.text: Saddles and takes horse about midnight

indicators.note: the riding word goes around the letter from the middle of night

parts.note: to take horse is to ride, so one who does so rides
the middle letter of the word night is G

explanation.surface: A rider saddles up and sets off on horseback around twelve at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saddles' looks like the verb for a horse; here it is the noun, the low ridge between two mountain peaks.
explanation.definitionFit: A saddle in geography is a dip between peaks, a kind of ridge, so saddles are crests of high ground.

clue.text: Two animals bound into cover

parts.note: a buck is a male deer, the first of the two animals
a ram is a male sheep, the second of the two animals

explanation.surface: Two beasts leap together into a hiding place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound' suggests the animals leaping, but buckram is a stiff cloth used to bind book covers.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckram is a stiffened coarse cloth used as a covering for books and for stiffening garments.

clue.text: Is perhaps disposed to produce objects of worth

indicators.note: disposed means arranged or set out, so the letters are placed in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is perhaps inclined to come up with valuable things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disposed' reads as 'inclined to', but it signals that IS PERHAPS is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: These blue gemstones are precious items of great value, so they are things of worth.

clue.text: Left society

parts.note: a member of a long-standing left-wing British socialist group named after a cautious Roman general

explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the past tense of leave, as if someone quit society; it is the political left.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of this British socialist group, founded in 1884, belong to a society of the political left.

clue.text: The better runners suffer setback at start of this race

definitions.text: The better runners suffer setback at start of this race

parts.words: The better runners suffer setback at start of this race
parts.note: a race in which stronger competitors carry extra weight or start further back to even out the field

explanation.walkthrough: 'setback' sounds like a misfortune, but here the better runners literally start further back.
explanation.definitionFit: In this kind of race the stronger runners are given a disadvantage so that all have a fair chance.

clue.text: Business studies

parts.note: studies carried out by a business into what customers want, not a school subject

explanation.walkthrough: 'Business studies' is a school and university subject; here it means surveys a business conducts.
explanation.definitionFit: Companies commission surveys of consumer needs and preferences, which are studies done for business purposes.

clue.text: Bat, net and lines set out for the game

indicators.note: set out means laid out afresh, so the letters are arranged in a new order

explanation.surface: Bat, net and court markings are laid out for a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set out' rearranges BAT, NET and LINES; 'and' joins them and gives no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ping-pong is a game, and bat, net and lines are all equipment from it.

clue.text: Unusual Biblical book required to make up set, perhaps

parts.note: unusual means odd
Numbers is the fourth book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A strange book of the Bible is needed to complete a collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set' is the mathematical sense: 1, 3, 5 and so on form a set.
explanation.definitionFit: The integers not divisible by two form a mathematical set, so they are an example of one.

clue.text: A composer frequently, we hear, supported by another

indicators.note: in a down clue the second composer sits below and so supports the first
we hear signals that the word for frequently is taken by how it sounds

parts.note: frequently means often, which some say with a silent T
another composer, J. S. Bach

explanation.surface: A composer who often appears beside a second one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' makes OFTEN sound like OFFEN; 'supported by' puts BACH beneath it in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacques Offenbach was a 19th-century French composer of operettas, such as Orpheus in the Underworld.

clue.text: Arab prince recalls Ancient Mariner story

indicators.note: recalls is read as calls back, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: Coleridge's poem is The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

explanation.surface: An Arab prince remembers Coleridge's famous sea poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalls' looks like remembering, but it means the poem's word RIME is turned back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim ruler or prince in Arab lands, a direct title for one.

clue.text: Head at first greatly put out by dullness

indicators.note: put out means disturbed, so the letters are thrown into disorder
at first means only the opening letter of the word head is taken

explanation.surface: A headmaster is very annoyed by a lack of liveliness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' gives H from 'Head' and 'put out' scrambles H with GREATLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Lethargy is sluggishness and lack of energy, which is dullness of body or mind.

clue.text: Craze beginning to ebb and die away

parts.note: a craze is a fad

indicators.note: beginning to means only the first letter of ebb is taken

explanation.surface: A fashion begins to wane and then disappears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to' takes only E from 'ebb'.
explanation.definitionFit: To fade is to grow gradually fainter until gone, which is to die away.

clue.text: Indicated it is not in action

indicators.note: the word not is placed inside the word for an action

parts.note: a deed is an action

explanation.surface: Someone signalled that something is not happening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it is' is a link here: the clue reads 'Indicated: it is not in action'.
explanation.definitionFit: To denote is to signify or point out, so denoted is a synonym of indicated.

clue.text: Insufficient quantity irritates general not long in his eating place

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go inside the dining room word

parts.note: a mess is the place where military officers eat

indicators.note: irritates is read as stirs up, so the letters are mixed
long is abbreviated L, and not removes that letter from general

explanation.surface: A general is annoyed by the poor portions served in his officers' dining room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'his eating place' refers back to the general: officers eat in a mess. The scrambled remainder is AGRENE.
explanation.definitionFit: Meagreness is scantiness or meanness of amount, so it is an insufficient quantity.

clue.text: Oval 45-inch mince pies

parts.note: an ell is an old English measure of cloth of 45 inches

indicators.note: to mince is to chop up, so the letters are cut and rearranged

explanation.surface: An oval tray of mince pies measuring forty-five inches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mince pies' looks like the Christmas treat, but 'mince' scrambles the second word to give the ending IPSE.
explanation.definitionFit: An ellipse is a regular oval shape, like a flattened circle.

clue.text: Good man gets response in church from organ

parts.note: a saint is a good man, abbreviated ST
amen is the congregation's response to a prayer

explanation.surface: A virtuous man hears the congregation answer him from the church organ.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' suggests the church instrument; it is the pollen-bearing part of a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The stamen is the male reproductive organ of a flower, which produces pollen.

clue.text: A bar, of course

parts.note: the clubhouse bar where golfers go after the eighteen holes of a golf course

explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally'; it means belonging to a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers jokingly call the clubhouse bar the hole after the last, where the round is celebrated.

clue.text: A French veto expected soon

parts.note: non is French for no

explanation.surface: A French refusal is anticipated shortly.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an old-fashioned word for shortly or in a little while.

clue.text: Element may be Athenian in any case

indicators.note: in and case together say one word is put inside another as in a casing
case means the outer word encloses the name

parts.note: Timon of Athens is the title character of a Shakespeare play

explanation.surface: An element might be Greek, whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in any case' looks like 'anyway', but the three-letter word is the case wrapped around the Athenian's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Antimony is a chemical element, a brittle silvery metalloid with symbol Sb.

clue.text: Saw the head for an examination

definitions.text: Saw the head for an examination

parts.words: Saw the head for an examination
parts.note: to cut a hole in the skull with a surgical saw, as for examining the brain

explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' could be the past tense of see, as if seeing the boss; it is the cutting verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons bore through the skull with a cylindrical saw to reach the brain, an operation of that name.

clue.text: The trouble about a Spaniard is he puts pleasure before work

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go around the Spaniard and is
trouble means disturb, so the letters of the first word are mixed

parts.note: don is a Spanish title for a gentleman

explanation.surface: The problem with a man from Spain is that he would rather enjoy himself than work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The trouble' looks like 'the problem'; it is the scrambling signal, making HET to be split around the Spaniard.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist is a pleasure-seeker, one who makes enjoyment the main aim of life.

clue.text: Different points about very unusual beast

indicators.note: the two compass letters go around the mixed letters

parts.note: W and N are two different compass points, west and north

indicators.note: unusual means out of the normal order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Directions are given around a most peculiar creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' makes YVER from VERY; 'about' places W and N on either side.
explanation.definitionFit: A wyvern is a heraldic winged dragon with two legs, a mythical beast.
